case_info.explanation: Dual atrioventricular nodal nonreentrant tachycardia Initially, ECG recordings were interpreted as focal atrial tachycardia or paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, often observed in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy. Hence, some cardiologists suggested starting oral anticoagulant therapy and considering pulmonary vein isolation, which may be beneficial in patients with heart failure.1Moreover, based on the severe left ventricular dysfunction without apparent reversible causes and suspected nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, defibrillator implantation (primary prevention) would be reasonable if no clinical-echocardiographic improvement occurs following 3 months of optimal medical therapy.2Of note, correction of the significant functional mitral regurgitation (eg, transcatheter edge-to-edge repair) may also improve the patient’s symptoms and reduce the arrhythmia burden by reducing the hemodynamic stress on the left atrium.3 Nonetheless, careful analysis of the 12-lead ECG during the arrhythmia, focusing on the lead II rhythm strip, revealed an irregular but repetitive pattern during the arrhythmia, alternating between short and long RR intervals. Moreover, positive sinus P waves could be tracked throughout lead II at a relatively stable sinus rate of approximately 90 beats per minute (Figure 2A). These electrocardiographic features were incompatible with atrial fibrillation or atrial tachycardia (P waves < QRS complexes). Double firing over both the fast and slow nodal pathways was suspected during this arrhythmia, presenting as dual atrioventricular nodal nonreentrant tachycardia (DAVNNT).4Occasional block over the slow pathway or fast pathway occurred, observing 1:1 A:V conduction with normal or prolonged PR intervals, respectively. Nevertheless, the electrocardiographic differential diagnosis may still include repetitive junctional ectopic activity as the underlying mechanism. Of note, arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy was also suspected due to the incessant pattern of this arrhythmia with uncontrolled heart rates during Holter monitoring (arrhythmia burden, >50%).5 After obtaining patient informed consent, an electrophysiological study was performed. Multipolar diagnostic catheters were introduced through the femoral veins and positioned at the His bundle region, high right atrium, and within the coronary sinus. During the procedure under conscious sedation, short phases of stable sinus rhythm with 1:1 normal atrioventricular conduction were documented. Intracardiac recordings during arrhythmia (Figure 2B) revealed sinus atriograms (early atriograms at high right atrium), each followed by double ventricular depolarizations showing narrow QRS, normal HV interval, and physiologic His bundle activation sequence (ie, proximal to distal). These features highly suggested double nodal “firing” or DAVNNT.4Furthermore, atrial pacing confirmed the presence of dual antegrade nodal physiology, while atrial premature extrastimulation could reproducibly induce the 2:1 response (double firing), supporting the DAVNNT diagnosis. Conventional radiofrequency catheter ablation effectively eliminated the slow pathway and restored stable sinus rhythm. The patient remained asymptomatic during the successive 3-month follow-up. Holter-ECG revealed sinus rhythm without relevant arrhythmias, and the echocardiogram displayed near normalization of ejection fraction (50%) with trivial mitral regurgitation, confirming the initial diagnosis of arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy.5 In summary, this case highlights the crucial role of careful, in-depth analysis of the 12-lead ECG that may dramatically impact patient management and clinical outcomes.
